items.title: Global stocks tumble as AI panic grips markets after Democrats’ midterm success – business live
items.summary: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news, as Asia-Pacific markets slide after Wall Street rout The Financial Times have calculated that US stocks shed $3.2tn on Thursday, in a day of “chaotic trading”. Thet explain: The market value drop on the S&P Composite 1500 index, a broad basket of America’s publicly traded companies, was the biggest since the turn of the millennium, according to FT calculations based on FactSet data “(Clients) were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. “All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints, ... because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money. The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom. The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations. Earnings season has been an overall disappointment for the markets, with Magnificent Seven results so far undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down. 7am GMT: Lloyds house price index 9am GMT: UN’s FAO food price index 1.30pm GMT: US non-farm payrolls jobs report 3pm GMT: University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence report

items.title: Darwin-180B-RSI: How a 180B-Parameter Model Was Updated by Modifying Just 0.02% of Its Weights
items.summary: Darwin-180B-RSI: How a 180B-Parameter Model Was Updated by Modifying Just 0.02% of Its Weights TL;DR: VIDRAFT's Darwin-180B-RSI is a 180-billion-parameter model that was refreshed through a self-improvement (RSI) loop by updating a claimed 0.02% of its parameters — leaving the vast majority of the model frozen. Beyond the training methodology, the model is notable for running on consumer-grade laptop SSD storage via a streaming inference approach that achieves a reported 4.17 tokens/second. If you care about parameter-efficient self-improvement or commodity hardware deployment of frontier-scale models, this one is worth watching. What it is Darwin-180B-RSI is VIDRAFT's 180-billion-parameter language model, updated via a Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) cycle. The key claim from the source is surgical: rather than retraining the full model, the RSI update touched approximately 0.02% of the model's total parameters . The remaining ~99.98% of weights were kept frozen during the update pass. The second headline result is a hardware deployment story. Darwin-180B-RSI has been demonstrated running on a laptop with SSD-based weight streaming , achieving 4.17 tokens per second — a throughput figure that would have been implausible for a model of this scale on consumer hardware even a short time ago. Together, these two results position Darwin-180B-RSI at an interesting intersection: extremely sparse self-modification during training, and extremely lean resource requirements at inference. How it works Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) at a high level The RSI framing means the model participates in its own update cycle in some capacity — generating signals, critiques, or candidates that feed back into a targeted weight-update step. The 0.02% figure implies the update mechanism is highly localized: rather than broad gradient descent across all layers, only a small subset of parameters are identified as candidates for modification and updated. Conceptually, this is adjacent to techniques like sparse fine-tuning , parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) , and selective layer updating , but the RSI label suggests the selection or update signal itself originates (at least in part) from the model's own outputs rather than purely from an external labeled dataset. The exact mechanism for identifying which 0.02% of parameters to update is not disclosed in the source. SSD streaming inference Running 180 billion parameters on a laptop requires moving weights from storage into compute memory on demand rather than holding the full model in VRAM or RAM simultaneously. The 4.17 tok/s figure is what the source reports for this streaming configuration. This approach trades peak throughput for accessibility — making a frontier-scale model runnable without a multi-GPU server. This is conceptually similar to memory-mapped weight loading or quantized offloading strategies already present in the open-source ecosystem (think llama.cpp -style CPU/GPU offloading), applied here to a model an order of magnitude larger than typical open-weight community models. Benchmarks & results Based on what the source reports, the concrete figures are: Parameter update scope: ~0.02% of 180 billion parameters modified during the RSI update cycle SSD streaming inference throughput: 4.17 tokens/second on a laptop The source does not report standard leaderboard benchmark scores (e.g., MMLU, HumanEval, MT-Bench, or similar) in the excerpted content available. Qualitatively, the framing from iTechGuides positions this as a technically novel result for the efficiency of the update method and the accessibility of the deployment target, rather than primarily a capability benchmark story. No additional public benchmark numbers are available from this source, and none will be invented here. How to try it The source article does not include explicit public access instructions — no Hugging Face repository URL, GitHub link, or API endpoint is confirmed in the available content. Based on VIDRAFT's previously established developer channels (consistent with their other Darwin-series releases), you may want to monitor: Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/vidraft — VIDRAFT has used this organization page for prior model releases VIDRAFT's official channels for announcements about Darwin-180B-RSI availability If and when a public model card or API is announced, standard access patterns for OpenAI-compatible endpoints would apply (e.g., pointing an OpenAI SDK client at the announced base URL with your API key). No specific endpoint, model name string, or access token format is confirmed public at this time, so no shell commands are included here to avoid directing you to an endpoint that may not yet exist. Check the source article directly for the most current access information: itechguides.com/darwin-180b-rsi-... FAQ Q: Does updating only 0.02% of parameters actually constitute meaningful self-improvement, or is this just a fine-tuning pass? A: That's the technically interesting question. The RSI label implies the update signal has a self-referential component — the model's own outputs contribute to determining what gets updated — which distinguishes it conceptually from a standard supervised fine-tuning pass on external data. Whether the 0.02% threshold represents a deliberate architectural constraint or an emergent result of the update method isn't specified in the source. Q: Is 4.17 tok/s on a laptop actually usable for development or just a benchmark curiosity? A: For interactive use, 4.17 tok/s is on the slower end — roughly comparable to a fast human reading speed — but it's functional for batch inference, offline experimentation, or scenarios where GPU server access isn't available. For a 180B-parameter model on consumer hardware, it's a meaningful engineering result regardless of whether it matches server-grade throughput. Beyond the training methodology, the model is notable for running on consumer-grade laptop SSD storage via a streaming inference approach that achieves a reported 4.17 tokens/second. If you care about parameter-efficient self-improvement or commodity hardware deployment of frontier-scale models, this one is worth watching.

What it is

Darwin-180B-RSI is VIDRAFT's 180-billion-parameter language model, updated via a Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) cycle. The key claim from the source is surgical: rather than retraining the full model, the RSI update touched approximately 0.02% of the model's total parameters. The remaining ~99.98% of weights were kept frozen during the update pass.

The second headline result is a hardware deployment story. Darwin-180B-RSI has been demonstrated running on a laptop with SSD-based weight streaming, achieving 4.17 tokens per second — a throughput figure that would have been implausible for a model of this scale on consumer hardware even a short time ago.

Together, these two results position Darwin-180B-RSI at an interesting intersection: extremely sparse self-modification during training, and extremely lean resource requirements at inference.

How it works Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) at a high level

The RSI framing means the model participates in its own update cycle in some capacity — generating signals, critiques, or candidates that feed back into a targeted weight-update step. The 0.02% figure implies the update mechanism is highly localized: rather than broad gradient descent across all layers, only a small subset of parameters are identified as candidates for modification and updated.

Conceptually, this is adjacent to techniques like sparse fine-tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), and selective layer updating, but the RSI label suggests the selection or update signal itself originates (at least in part) from the model's own outputs rather than purely from an external labeled dataset. The exact mechanism for identifying which 0.02% of parameters to update is not disclosed in the source.

SSD streaming inference

Running 180 billion parameters on a laptop requires moving weights from storage into compute memory on demand rather than holding the full model in VRAM or RAM simultaneously. The 4.17 tok/s figure is what the source reports for this streaming configuration. This approach trades peak throughput for accessibility — making a frontier-scale model runnable without a multi-GPU server.

This is conceptually similar to memory-mapped weight loading or quantized offloading strategies already present in the open-source ecosystem (think llama.cpp-style CPU/GPU offloading), applied here to a model an order of magnitude larger than typical open-weight community models.

items.title: Scientist World turns 1,000 papers into executable research environments
items.summary: Researchers propose Scientist World, a pipeline that converts papers into executable environments by extracting open-ended research questions and reproducing authors' methods as baselines. AI scientists are then scored against human results. The first 1,000 verified environments are released. Why it matters It gives AI scientists a standard, runnable testbed for open-ended research, rather than static benchmarks or isolated tasks. Analysis Scientist World converts papers into environments with human baselines, enabling direct comparison of AI and human research. That could make progress in automated science measurable and cumulative. The main uncertainty is quality: automatic extraction and reproduction may introduce errors, narrow questions, or leak solutions, limiting validity at scale. Source: arXiv AI disclosure: this article was produced with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy.

items.title: Two Agents Both Added a Package: 7 Lockfiles and the Command That Fixes Each Conflict
items.summary: Book: AI Agents Pocket Guide Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub The second branch stops at package-lock.json . Two agents worked in two worktrees: one added a validation library, the other a date library. Each ran an install and passed its tests, and the first branch merged cleanly. Often the manifest conflicts too, because both agents added a line to the same dependencies block. Parallel agents make this routine. Every task that touches dependencies rewrites the same generated file, and git can't merge a generated file line by line with any confidence. Six of the seven package managers below document a fix, most of them a single command, and the seventh needs a short manual routine. Each one links to the tool's own docs. The rule that covers all seven Fix the manifest by hand. Never hand-edit the lockfile. package.json , composer.json , go.mod and Cargo.toml are files you own, so you decide which lines both branches keep. The lockfile is output, and the package manager should write it. When the fix below says "take one side first", know which side is which. In a merge into main , --ours is main , the branch you're on, and --theirs is the branch coming in. In a rebase git swaps the labels: the git-checkout docs say --ours then "gives the version from the branch the changes are rebased onto". So when you rebase your branch onto main , --ours is still main 's copy. Taking the target branch's lockfile keeps every version that has already landed, and the install adds only what the incoming branch brought. Two installs, one generated file: the lockfile is where parallel branches meet first. JavaScript: npm, pnpm, Yarn and Bun 1. npm ( package-lock.json ). npm's docs say that since npm@5.7.0 you can resolve these conflicts "by manually fixing any package.json conflicts, and then running npm install [--package-lock-only] again". npm then writes a merged lock "that includes all the dependencies from both branches". The flag skips touching node_modules/ . # package.json fixed by hand, then: npm install --package-lock-only git add package.json package-lock.json To check the result, npm ci exits with an error if the lock doesn't match package.json , instead of updating it. 2. pnpm ( pnpm-lock.yaml ). pnpm's docs say it "can automatically resolve merge conflicts in pnpm-lock.yaml ". Run pnpm install and commit. If both sides are valid lockfiles, pnpm merges them. If not, it fails with a parse error, so read the result before you commit. pnpm install git add pnpm-lock.yaml 3. Yarn Berry ( yarn.lock ). Yarn detects conflict markers on install and logs YN0049 AUTOMERGE_REQUIRED . Its heuristic takes the lockfile from the pulled branch, adds your branch's entries and installs again. When that works you get YN0048 AUTOMERGE_SUCCESS . Two failure modes are worth knowing. Under --immutable (typical in CI) Yarn refuses to edit the file and reports YN0047 , so run the install locally. If someone committed the lockfile with markers still in it, Yarn can't find the two versions to merge ( YN0083 ); revert the lockfile to a working version and install again. yarn install # without --immutable git add yarn.lock 4. Bun ( bun.lock ). Bun switched its default to the text bun.lock in v1.2, and the announcement gives merge conflicts as one reason: binary lockfiles made them "harder to resolve". Bun's lockfile docs don't describe automatic conflict resolution, so I wouldn't count on it. Take the target branch's copy and let the install add what the manifest now asks for. git checkout --ours bun.lock # main's copy bun install git add bun.lock One caveat for this one: the incoming branch's new package gets resolved again, so it can land on a newer version than the one the agent tested with. Read the lockfile diff. PHP, Go and Rust 5. Composer ( composer.lock ). If the only conflict is the content-hash line, Composer's guide says composer update --lock "may be enough to remove the conflict marker". The CLI reference describes --lock as overwriting the hash "without updating package versions". For real conflicts, the guide says to accept both files from the branch with the most changes, then re-run the other branch's changes as commands: git checkout --ours composer.json composer.lock # more changes composer require vendor/package composer validate Use --theirs instead if the other side changed more, then require what the side you dropped had added. composer validate checks that the lock is up to date with composer.json . The guide warns that re-requiring a package can pick a newer version than the other branch had locked. 6. Go ( go.sum ). Resolve go.mod by hand: keep both require lines. For go.sum , keeping both sides' lines is safe, because the Go reference says the file "may contain hashes for multiple versions of a module". Then tidy, which "will add missing hashes and will remove unnecessary hashes from go.sum ": # go.mod fixed by hand, markers removed go mod tidy git add go.mod go.sum In CI, go mod tidy -diff changes nothing and exits non-zero if the files are not tidy. 7. Cargo ( Cargo.lock ). Cargo's guide says Cargo.lock "is maintained by Cargo and should not be manually edited". Fix Cargo.toml , take the target branch's lock, then update the workspace. The --workspace flag updates only your own crates, and other packages "are updated only if they don't already exist in the lockfile", so the incoming dependency gets added and everything already locked stays put. git checkout --ours Cargo.lock # main's copy cargo update --workspace git add Cargo.toml Cargo.lock cargo build --locked in CI fails if Cargo would have to change the lock. For teams that hit this daily: merge drivers and branch lockfiles If you land five agent branches a day, a manual step per conflict adds up. Three options, from narrowest to broadest. Union merge for go.sum . git's built-in union driver takes lines from both versions instead of writing conflict markers. That suits a file that is a set of hash lines. The git docs warn the lines can come out "in random order and the user should verify the result", so run go mod tidy after the merge. # .gitattributes go.sum merge=union Branch lockfiles in pnpm. With gitBranchLockfile: true in pnpm-workspace.yaml , each branch writes its own pnpm-lock. .yaml , so branches never touch the same file. pnpm install --merge-git-branch-lockfiles folds them back into pnpm-lock.yaml and deletes the branch files, and mergeGitBranchLockfilesBranchPattern makes that happen on its own on branches such as main . A custom driver. git lets you register any command as a merge driver in .git/config and map files to it in .gitattributes . The gitattributes docs define the contract: the command gets %O (ancestor), %A (current) and %B (other), writes the result into %A , and exits zero for a clean merge. npm's v6 docs point at npm-merge-driver for this, but that repository was archived in August 2021 and is read-only, so plan on maintaining your own if you go this way. Land one branch at a time, and fix the lock on the branch The habit that makes all seven fixes painless: land the first branch, then rebase the second onto the new main inside its own worktree, fix the lockfile there and run its tests before it merges. The conflict gets resolved on a branch where a broken install costs nothing, not on main . cd ~/code/app-add-dates git rebase main # fix package.json by hand, then: npm install --package-lock-only git add package.json package-lock.json git rebase --continue That second-worktree step is where Hermes IDE fits. I build it, so weigh this with that in mind. Each task you start with ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) runs on its own hermes/ branch in its own worktree, so each agent's install stays on its branch until you land it. The Review Desk (⌘G) shows each task's changes by turn or by file, with risk flags. Land then commits, opens a pull request or merges locally, into the branch the task started from, one task at a time, and it can be undone. The Review Desk's Worktrees tab: one Hermes worktree per task, each with its hermes/ branch, task, age and disk size. You can also make the lockfile part of "done". A worktree recipe in .hermes/worktree.toml takes done_when checks, the default checks for when a task is done. Put the strict install there, and the task isn't done until npm ci passes against the lockfile: # .hermes/worktree.toml setup = [ "npm ci" ] done_when = [ "npm ci" , "npm test" ] Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It isn't affiliated with Anthropic, OpenAI or any agent vendor. Download it or read the code on GitHub . The cheat-sheet Lockfile After fixing the manifest CI check package-lock.json npm install --package-lock-only npm ci pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm install Read the diff yarn.lock (Berry) yarn install yarn install --immutable bun.lock --ours lock, then bun install Read the diff composer.lock composer update --lock or re- require composer validate go.sum go mod tidy go mod tidy -diff Cargo.lock --ours lock, cargo update --workspace cargo build --locked --ours is main 's copy whether you merge into main or rebase onto it. Use --theirs only when you merge main into your branch. If this was useful Lockfile conflicts are one small symptom of a bigger question: how you split work between agents so their output can be merged at all. My AI Agents Pocket Guide covers that side: multi-agent orchestration, the guardrails around what an agent may change, and how to keep autonomous work reviewable. If you run Hermes, the worktree recipe above is a one-file way to start.

Union merge for go.sum. git's built-in union driver takes lines from both versions instead of writing conflict markers. That suits a file that is a set of hash lines. The git docs warn the lines can come out "in random order and the user should verify the result", so run go mod tidy after the merge.

# .gitattributes
go.sum merge=union

Branch lockfiles in pnpm. With gitBranchLockfile: true in pnpm-workspace.yaml, each branch writes its own pnpm-lock..yaml, so branches never touch the same file. pnpm install --merge-git-branch-lockfiles folds them back into pnpm-lock.yaml and deletes the branch files, and mergeGitBranchLockfilesBranchPattern makes that happen on its own on branches such as main.

A custom driver. git lets you register any command as a merge driver in .git/config and map files to it in .gitattributes. The gitattributes docs define the contract: the command gets %O (ancestor), %A (current) and %B (other), writes the result into %A, and exits zero for a clean merge. npm's v6 docs point at npm-merge-driver for this, but that repository was archived in August 2021 and is read-only, so plan on maintaining your own if you go this way.

Land one branch at a time, and fix the lock on the branch

The habit that makes all seven fixes painless: land the first branch, then rebase the second onto the new main inside its own worktree, fix the lockfile there and run its tests before it merges. The conflict gets resolved on a branch where a broken install costs nothing, not on main.

cd ~/code/app-add-dates
git rebase main
# fix package.json by hand, then:
npm install --package-lock-only
git add package.json package-lock.json
git rebase --continue

That second-worktree step is where Hermes IDE fits. I build it, so weigh this with that in mind. Each task you start with ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) runs on its own hermes/ branch in its own worktree, so each agent's install stays on its branch until you land it. The Review Desk (⌘G) shows each task's changes by turn or by file, with risk flags. Land then commits, opens a pull request or merges locally, into the branch the task started from, one task at a time, and it can be undone.


The Review Desk's Worktrees tab: one Hermes worktree per task, each with its hermes/ branch, task, age and disk size.

You can also make the lockfile part of "done". A worktree recipe in .hermes/worktree.toml takes done_when checks, the default checks for when a task is done. Put the strict install there, and the task isn't done until npm ci passes against the lockfile:

# .hermes/worktree.toml
setup = ["npm ci"]
done_when = ["npm ci", "npm test"]

Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It isn't affiliated with Anthropic, OpenAI or any agent vendor. Download it or read the code on GitHub.

The cheat-sheet
Lockfile After fixing the manifest CI check package-lock.json npm install --package-lock-only npm ci pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm install Read the diff yarn.lock (Berry) yarn install yarn install --immutable bun.lock --ours lock, then bun install Read the diff composer.lock composer update --lock or re-require composer validate go.sum go mod tidy go mod tidy -diff Cargo.lock --ours lock, cargo update --workspace cargo build --locked

--ours is main's copy whether you merge into main or rebase onto it. Use --theirs only when you merge main into your branch.

If this was useful

Lockfile conflicts are one small symptom of a bigger question: how you split work between agents so their output can be merged at all. My AI Agents Pocket Guide covers that side: multi-agent orchestration, the guardrails around what an agent may change, and how to keep autonomous work reviewable. If you run Hermes, the worktree recipe above is a one-file way to start.

items.title: Count outcomes, not agents
items.summary: When organisations start working with AI agents, progress is often reported as a count of agents built. The count is easy to measure, but it says little about whether the work has improved. Measure the work, not the agents. Before any agent goes live, record three or four measures for the process it will touch. Good candidates are: cycle time; rework or error rate; cost per case; customer satisfaction. These measures become the baseline. Pilot one step. Choose a single step in the process. Let an agent draft or prepare the work, and have people review every case. This keeps quality visible from the first day. Compare like with like. After a set period, take the same measures again. If the step is faster, more accurate or cheaper, you have evidence. If it isn't, you have learned something useful at low cost. Count the full running cost. The business case should include: model usage; the time people spend reviewing; monitoring; the effort of changing the process. A pilot that looks inexpensive can be costly to run at scale, and the reverse can also be true. Fund in stages. Release the next budget when the last stage has shown its value. This keeps decisions grounded, and it gives finance, operations and technology teams a shared view of progress. A short checklist: Do you have a baseline for the process before the agent arrives? Is every pilot reviewed by people until the evidence is in? Does your business case include the cost of review and monitoring? From the 2SD Technologies team ( 2sdtechnologies.com ). Part 4 of "Don't just build agents".

items.title: MCP Went Stateless This Year. Your 'Supports MCP' Checkbox Is Now a Lie.
items.summary: MCP Went Stateless This Year. Your "Supports MCP" Checkbox Is Now a Lie. "We support MCP" used to mean something specific. This year it became ambiguous, because there are now effectively two MCPs, and most vendors aren't telling you which one they mean. The protocol is a year old and already halfway through its own identity crisis. If you build or buy anything agent-adjacent, this is your migration, whether or not anyone scheduled it. And nobody scheduled it. What changed The 2026-07-28 spec revision is the biggest change since the protocol launched, and the headline is: the session is gone. Before: a client called initialize , got a session ID, and got pinned to one server instance. Scaling meant sticky routing or a shared session store like Redis, which meant every request depended on the store, one instance dying took its sessions with it, and load balancing was a permanent geometric pain. After: every request carries what it needs. No handshake, no session, no sticky routing. A plain round-robin load balancer in front of stateless servers, and a server restart stops being an event. There's more in the revision, authorization tightened up toward OAuth and OIDC conventions, a deprecation policy, extensions for long-running work and server-rendered UIs. But statelessness is the one that rewrites your infrastructure assumptions. Why it matters beyond hygiene: the scale signal is absurd. The protocol's own tier-one SDKs are logging on the order of half a billion monthly downloads, TypeScript and Python past a billion lifetime each. "Supports MCP" is no longer a boutique claim. Which cuts both ways, because an ambiguous checkbox on a spec that large is a very big ambiguous checkbox. The migration nobody budgeted Here's the part that will eat afternoons: the change is breaking, and the ecosystem is straddling it. Two generations of MCP are live in production right now. Some clients are on old SDKs. Some servers expect the old handshake. "We support MCP" can mean either revision, and nothing in the phrase tells you which. For a while, buying agent tooling is going to be like buying a USB device with no marking on the connector. The checklist that saves the migration: Find the revision before anything else. Probe for initialize and see what happens. Old revision answers, new revision doesn't expect it. This one diagnostic sorts your whole vendor list. Drop sticky routing on new-revision servers. Round-robin is the whole point. If you're on old-revision servers, you still need sessions and this paragraph doesn't apply yet, and knowing which side of that you're on is the actual work. Re-verify auth flows on both generations. This is where the afternoons go: a client that "works" against new-revision servers fails silently against old ones, because the handshake it skipped was load-bearing for the old auth path. The failure looks like your bug. It's a version mismatch. Pin SDK versions and record which revision they speak. The ambiguity doesn't resolve itself, it gets managed. A two-column list, servers and their revision, is the entire artifact. The part I actually like I keep this honest by noting what's genuinely good here: stateless MCP is simpler, and the direction is right. Simon Willison made the case when the spec landed, tooling that speaks MCP is auditable in a way a shell-enabled agent isn't, and the stateless core means the protocol scales on boring infrastructure that every ops team already owns. It moved toward how CLIs have always worked: run a command, get output, move on. The pain is transitional, not architectural. That's rare and worth saying out loud, because most breaking migrations are pain all the way down. What I can't claim The old generation isn't going anywhere fast. Some hosts will be stuck on old SDKs for a long time, and straddling is going to be the normal condition, not a phase. Plan for living in ambiguity, not for graduating out of it. And a checkbox is still a checkbox: even when your vendor names their revision, someone has to verify, because support matrices rot and spec revisions keep coming. Trust the probe, not the label. Stop asking vendors "do you support MCP." Ask "which revision," and keep the probe in a script, because the answer changes faster than the docs. Which revision is your MCP server actually speaking, and when did you last check rather than assume?

MCP Went Stateless This Year. Your "Supports MCP" Checkbox Is Now a Lie.

"We support MCP" used to mean something specific. This year it became ambiguous, because there are now effectively two MCPs, and most vendors aren't telling you which one they mean.

The protocol is a year old and already halfway through its own identity crisis.

If you build or buy anything agent-adjacent, this is your migration, whether or not anyone scheduled it. And nobody scheduled it.

What changed

The 2026-07-28 spec revision is the biggest change since the protocol launched, and the headline is: the session is gone.

Before: a client called initialize, got a session ID, and got pinned to one server instance. Scaling meant sticky routing or a shared session store like Redis, which meant every request depended on the store, one instance dying took its sessions with it, and load balancing was a permanent geometric pain.

After: every request carries what it needs. No handshake, no session, no sticky routing. A plain round-robin load balancer in front of stateless servers, and a server restart stops being an event.

There's more in the revision, authorization tightened up toward OAuth and OIDC conventions, a deprecation policy, extensions for long-running work and server-rendered UIs. But statelessness is the one that rewrites your infrastructure assumptions.

Why it matters beyond hygiene: the scale signal is absurd. The protocol's own tier-one SDKs are logging on the order of half a billion monthly downloads, TypeScript and Python past a billion lifetime each. "Supports MCP" is no longer a boutique claim. Which cuts both ways, because an ambiguous checkbox on a spec that large is a very big ambiguous checkbox.

The migration nobody budgeted

Here's the part that will eat afternoons: the change is breaking, and the ecosystem is straddling it.

Two generations of MCP are live in production right now. Some clients are on old SDKs. Some servers expect the old handshake. "We support MCP" can mean either revision, and nothing in the phrase tells you which. For a while, buying agent tooling is going to be like buying a USB device with no marking on the connector.

The checklist that saves the migration:

Find the revision before anything else. Probe for initialize and see what happens. Old revision answers, new revision doesn't expect it. This one diagnostic sorts your whole vendor list.

Drop sticky routing on new-revision servers. Round-robin is the whole point. If you're on old-revision servers, you still need sessions and this paragraph doesn't apply yet, and knowing which side of that you're on is the actual work.

Re-verify auth flows on both generations. This is where the afternoons go: a client that "works" against new-revision servers fails silently against old ones, because the handshake it skipped was load-bearing for the old auth path. The failure looks like your bug. It's a version mismatch.

Pin SDK versions and record which revision they speak. The ambiguity doesn't resolve itself, it gets managed. A two-column list, servers and their revision, is the entire artifact.

The part I actually like

I keep this honest by noting what's genuinely good here: stateless MCP is simpler, and the direction is right. Simon Willison made the case when the spec landed, tooling that speaks MCP is auditable in a way a shell-enabled agent isn't, and the stateless core means the protocol scales on boring infrastructure that every ops team already owns. It moved toward how CLIs have always worked: run a command, get output, move on.

The pain is transitional, not architectural. That's rare and worth saying out loud, because most breaking migrations are pain all the way down.

What I can't claim

The old generation isn't going anywhere fast. Some hosts will be stuck on old SDKs for a long time, and straddling is going to be the normal condition, not a phase. Plan for living in ambiguity, not for graduating out of it.

And a checkbox is still a checkbox: even when your vendor names their revision, someone has to verify, because support matrices rot and spec revisions keep coming. Trust the probe, not the label.

Stop asking vendors "do you support MCP." Ask "which revision," and keep the probe in a script, because the answer changes faster than the docs.

Which revision is your MCP server actually speaking, and when did you last check rather than assume?

items.title: Top 10 PostgreSQL Production Outages & SRE Incident Troubleshooting Runbooks
items.summary: Top 10 PostgreSQL Production Outages & SRE Incident Troubleshooting Runbooks Introduction PostgreSQL is one of the most widely adopted open-source relational database systems, powering applications ranging from startups and SaaS platforms to large-scale enterprise infrastructure. However, running PostgreSQL in production introduces challenges that go beyond writing SQL queries and designing database schemas. A sudden database outage can cause application downtime, failed transactions, delayed background jobs, broken APIs, and even data loss. Sometimes, the database remains technically available but becomes so slow that applications experience timeouts and users cannot complete their operations. For Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), Database Administrators (DBAs), and backend engineers, understanding how to identify, troubleshoot, and recover from PostgreSQL incidents is essential. 🚀 Keep Learning with DevsCampus Technology evolves continuously, and staying updated with practical engineering knowledge is essential for every developer. At DevsCampus , we publish technical articles, engineering tutorials, and learning resources covering PostgreSQL, Database Engineering, DevOps, Cloud Computing, System Design, Artificial Intelligence, and emerging technologies. Whether you are a student preparing for a software engineering career or an experienced developer looking to strengthen your technical skills, DevsCampus helps you explore concepts, understand real-world engineering challenges, and keep up with the latest technology trends. Explore these resources to continue learning: PostgreSQL Engineering Articles – Explore PostgreSQL architecture, implementation, and production best practices. SQL Learning Hub – Learn SQL, database design, indexing, query optimization, and production database engineering. Visit DevsCampus.com to read more technical articles, explore practical tutorials, and stay updated with the latest developments in technology. Now, let's explore the 10 most common PostgreSQL production outages , their root causes, and practical SRE troubleshooting runbooks that engineers can use to investigate and resolve real-world incidents. Whether you manage PostgreSQL on Kubernetes, AWS RDS, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, or self-hosted Linux servers, these runbooks will help you respond to production incidents systematically. 1. PostgreSQL Connection Pool Exhaustion Incident Scenario Your application suddenly starts returning errors: FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections Your API response times increase, background workers stop processing jobs, and new application connections fail. Root Cause PostgreSQL has a configured maximum number of concurrent connections. The following configuration controls the connection limit: SHOW max_connections ; Common causes include: Application connection leaks. Too many application instances. Incorrect connection pool configuration. Long-running transactions. Background workers opening excessive connections. Missing connection pooling. SRE Troubleshooting Runbook Step 1: Check active connections SELECT state , COUNT ( * ) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state ; Step 2: Identify applications consuming connections SELECT application_name , client_addr , state , COUNT ( * ) AS connections FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY application_name , client_addr , state ORDER BY connections DESC ; Step 3: Identify long-running connections SELECT pid , usename , application_name , state , now () - query_start AS duration , query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY duration DESC ; Step 4: Terminate confirmed problematic sessions SELECT pg_terminate_backend ( 12345 ); Replace 12345 with the actual process ID after verifying that terminating the session is safe. Recovery Strategy Configure connection pooling using PgBouncer. Set appropriate application pool limits. Implement connection timeouts. Close unused connections. Investigate connection leaks. Monitor active connections against max_connections . Production Prevention: Establish connection budgets across all application instances rather than allowing every service to independently consume the entire database connection limit. Related Reading: Explore PostgreSQL engineering resources on DevsCampus to learn more about PostgreSQL architecture, connection management, and production database operations. 2. PostgreSQL High CPU Utilization Incident Scenario The PostgreSQL server suddenly reaches 95–100% CPU utilization. Applications become slow, API requests time out, and database queries take significantly longer than usual. Root Cause High CPU utilization can result from: Missing database indexes. Expensive JOIN operations. Inefficient SQL queries. Large sequential scans. Excessive concurrent queries. Poor query execution plans. Incorrect database statistics. SRE Troubleshooting Runbook Step 1: Identify expensive queries SELECT pid , now () - query_start AS duration , state , query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' ORDER BY duration DESC ; Step 2: Identify frequently executed expensive queries If pg_stat_statements is enabled: SELECT query , calls , total_exec_time , mean_exec_time , rows FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10 ; Step 3: Analyze the execution plan EXPLAIN ( ANALYZE , BUFFERS ) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1001 ; Remember that EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query. Exercise caution with expensive queries and statements that modify data. Step 4: Check server CPU usage top Or: htop Recovery Strategy Identify and optimize expensive queries. Add appropriate indexes. Update database statistics using ANALYZE . Reduce unnecessary query concurrency. Review execution plans. Consider read replicas for read-heavy workloads. Production Prevention: Monitor query execution time, CPU utilization, and database workload continuously. Related Reading: Learn how production database schemas influence query performance and scalability in Production Database Design on DevsCampus . 3. PostgreSQL Disk Space Exhaustion Incident Scenario Your application starts reporting database write failures: ERROR: could not extend file No space left on device Insert and update operations begin failing. PostgreSQL may also experience problems writing WAL files or temporary query files. Root Cause Common causes include: Rapid database growth. Unbounded application logs. Large temporary files. WAL accumulation. Failed replication slots retaining WAL. Missing WAL archiving cleanup. Large database indexes. Long-running transactions preventing cleanup. SRE Troubleshooting Runbook Step 1: Check available disk space df -h Step 2: Identify large directories sudo du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/ * Adjust the PostgreSQL data directory according to your installation. Step 3: Check database sizes SELECT datname , pg_size_pretty ( pg_database_size ( datname )) AS size FROM pg_database ORDER BY pg_database_size ( datname ) DESC ; Step 4: Check WAL directory size sudo du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/ * /pg_wal Step 5: Check replication slots SELECT slot_name , active , restart_lsn , pg_wal_lsn_diff ( pg_current_wal_lsn (), restart_lsn ) AS retained_wal_bytes FROM pg_replication_slots ; Recovery Strategy Expand the underlying storage volume. Investigate inactive replication slots. Correct WAL archiving failures. Review temporary file generation. Remove only confirmed obsolete files through supported PostgreSQL maintenance procedures. Implement database growth alerts. Critical Warning: Never manually delete files from PostgreSQL's pg_wal directory. Doing so can cause database corruption or prevent PostgreSQL from starting. Production Prevention: Configure disk usage alerts at 70%, 80%, and 90% capacity. 4. PostgreSQL Replication Lag Incident Scenario Your production application uses PostgreSQL primary-replica architecture. The primary database processes writes successfully, but read replicas return outdated data. Users update their profiles but continue seeing old information. Root Cause Replication lag can occur because of: Network latency. High write throughput. Slow replica storage. Long-running queries on replicas. Replication conflicts. Insufficient replica resources. WAL receiver or replay delays. SRE Troubleshooting Runbook Step 1: Check replication status on the primary SELECT application_name , client_addr , state , sync_state , write_lag , flush_lag , replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication ; Step 2: Check replication status on the replica SELECT pg_is_in_recovery (), pg_last_wal_receive_lsn (), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn (); Step 3: Calculate replay delay SELECT now () - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp () AS replication_delay ; This timestamp-based calculation is most meaningful when the primary is actively committing transactions. Recovery Strategy Investigate network connectivity. Increase replica compute and storage capacity where necessary. Optimize queries running on replicas. Investigate WAL receiver and replay activity. Review replication configuration. Temporarily route consistency-sensitive reads to the primary. Production Prevention: Monitor replication lag and establish thresholds that trigger alerts before application consistency is affected. 5. PostgreSQL Deadlocks Incident Scenario Your application starts reporting transaction failures: ERROR: deadlock detected DETAIL: Process 1234 waits for ShareLock on transaction 5678 Multiple transactions are waiting for resources held by each other. Root Cause A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions wait indefinitely for locks held by one another. Example: Transaction A: BEGIN ; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 ; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2 ; COMMIT ; Transaction B: BEGIN ; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 2 ; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE id = 1 ; COMMIT ; Both transactions acquire locks in different orders, potentially creating a deadlock. SRE Troubleshooting Runbook Step 1: Inspect database locks SELECT locktype , relation :: regclass , mode , granted , pid FROM pg_locks ORDER BY pid ; Step 2: Identify blocked queries SELECT pid , pg_blocking_pids ( pid ) AS blocking_pids , query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality ( pg_blocking_pids ( pid )) > 0 ; Step 3: Inspect PostgreSQL logs Look for: ERROR: deadlock detected Recovery Strategy Acquire database locks in a consistent order. Keep transactions short. Avoid unnecessary operations inside transactions. Implement application-level transaction retries. Review transaction isolation requirements. Production Prevention: Enable appropriate deadlock logging and monitor deadlock frequency. 6. PostgreSQL Slow Queries and Query Timeouts Incident Scenario Your application starts experiencing intermittent API failures: ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout Some database queries take several seconds or even minutes to complete. Root Cause Common reasons include: Missing indexes. Inefficient joins. Large table scans. Outdated database statistics. Lock contention. Excessive sorting. Poor pagination strategies. SRE Troubleshooting Runbook Step 1: Find long-running queries SELECT pid , now () - query_start AS execution_time , wait_event_type , wait_event , query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' ORDER BY execution_time DESC ; Step 2: Analyze query execution EXPLAIN ( ANALYZE , BUFFERS ) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING' ; Step 3: Check table statistics SELECT relname , n_live_tup , n_dead_tup , last_analyze , last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables ; Step 4: Review timeout configuration SHOW statement_timeout ; SHOW lock_timeout ; SHOW idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ; Recovery Strategy Optimize problematic SQL. Add appropriate indexes. Review JOIN conditions. Update statistics. Investigate lock waits. Apply sensible timeout limits. Production Prevention: Use pg_stat_statements to identify queries with high total execution time and monitor query latency percentiles. Related Reading: Learn more about production schema design, indexing considerations, and query scalability in Production Database Design – DevsCampus . 7. PostgreSQL Database Crash or Unexpected Restart Incident Scenario Your production application suddenly loses database connectivity. Monitoring reports: Connection refused The PostgreSQL service is no longer accepting connections. Root Cause Possible causes include: Operating system out-of-memory termination. Hardware failures. Storage problems. PostgreSQL process crashes. Invalid configuration changes. Container or Kubernetes restarts. Host-level resource exhaustion. SRE Troubleshooting Runbook Step 1: Check PostgreSQL service status sudo systemctl status postgresql Step 2: Inspect recent PostgreSQL logs sudo journalctl -u postgresql \ --since "30 minutes ago" Depending on the distribution, PostgreSQL logs may also be available under: /var/log/postgresql/ Step 3: Check memory utilization free -h Step 4: Check kernel OOM events dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'oom|killed process' Step 5: Check storage health df -h Recovery Strategy Identify the actual crash reason before restarting repeatedly. Verify storage availability. Check memory and CPU pressure. Review PostgreSQL recovery logs. Restore service after confirming the underlying issue is resolved. Validate application connectivity and transaction processing. Production Prevention: Implement database health checks, infrastructure monitoring, automated backups, and tested recovery procedures. 8. PostgreSQL VACUUM Problems and Table Bloat Incident Scenario Your database size keeps increasing even though application data is not growing significantly. Queries become slower, indexes grow larger, and disk utilization increases. Root Cause PostgreSQL uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) to manage concurrent transactions. Updates and deletes create obsolete row versions that must eventually be cleaned up by VACUUM. Table bloat can increase when: Autovacuum is disabled or incorrectly configured. Long-running transactions prevent cleanup. High update/delete workloads generate dead tuples. Autovacuum cannot keep up with table modifications. Replication slots or standby feedback retain old row versions. SRE Troubleshooting Runbook Step 1: Identify tables with dead tuples SELECT relname , n_live_tup , n_dead_tup , last_vacuum , last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10 ; Step 2: Inspect autovacuum configuration SHOW autovacuum ; SHOW autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor ; SHOW autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor ; Step 3: Identify long-running transactions SELECT pid , usename , state , now () - xact_start AS transaction_duration , query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY transaction_duration DESC ; Recovery Strategy Investigate long-running transactions. Ensure autovacuum is enabled. Tune autovacuum for large and frequently updated tables. Run targeted VACUUM operations where appropriate. VACUUM ( ANALYZE ) orders ; For severe table bloat, evaluate specialized maintenance approaches such as pg_repack , accounting for locking, disk-space, and operational requirements. Production Prevention: Monitor dead tuples, autovacuum activity, transaction age, and table growth. Related Reading: PostgreSQL maintenance is essential for preventing table bloat and keeping query performance stable. Explore Database Maintenance on DevsCampus to understand VACUUM, ANALYZE, index maintenance, and database statistics in greater detail. 9. PostgreSQL WAL Growth and Checkpoint Problems Incident Scenario Your database experiences increased disk utilization and write latency. PostgreSQL logs contain messages related to check

Top 10 PostgreSQL Production Outages & SRE Incident Troubleshooting Runbooks Introduction

PostgreSQL is one of the most widely adopted open-source relational database systems, powering applications ranging from startups and SaaS platforms to large-scale enterprise infrastructure.

However, running PostgreSQL in production introduces challenges that go beyond writing SQL queries and designing database schemas.

A sudden database outage can cause application downtime, failed transactions, delayed background jobs, broken APIs, and even data loss. Sometimes, the database remains technically available but becomes so slow that applications experience timeouts and users cannot complete their operations.

For Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), Database Administrators (DBAs), and backend engineers, understanding how to identify, troubleshoot, and recover from PostgreSQL incidents is essential.

🚀 Keep Learning with DevsCampus

Technology evolves continuously, and staying updated with practical engineering knowledge is essential for every developer.

At DevsCampus, we publish technical articles, engineering tutorials, and learning resources covering PostgreSQL, Database Engineering, DevOps, Cloud Computing, System Design, Artificial Intelligence, and emerging technologies.

Whether you are a student preparing for a software engineering career or an experienced developer looking to strengthen your technical skills, DevsCampus helps you explore concepts, understand real-world engineering challenges, and keep up with the latest technology trends.

Explore these resources to continue learning:

  • PostgreSQL Engineering Articles – Explore PostgreSQL architecture, implementation, and production best practices.
  • SQL Learning Hub – Learn SQL, database design, indexing, query optimization, and production database engineering.

Visit DevsCampus.com to read more technical articles, explore practical tutorials, and stay updated with the latest developments in technology.

Now, let's explore the 10 most common PostgreSQL production outages, their root causes, and practical SRE troubleshooting runbooks that engineers can use to investigate and resolve real-world incidents.

Whether you manage PostgreSQL on Kubernetes, AWS RDS, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, or self-hosted Linux servers, these runbooks will help you respond to production incidents systematically.

1. PostgreSQL Connection Pool Exhaustion Incident Scenario

Your application suddenly starts returning errors:

FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved
for non-replication superuser connections

Your API response times increase, background workers stop processing jobs, and new application connections fail.

Root Cause

PostgreSQL has a configured maximum number of concurrent connections.

The following configuration controls the connection limit:

SHOW max_connections;

Common causes include:

  • Application connection leaks.
  • Too many application instances.
  • Incorrect connection pool configuration.
  • Long-running transactions.
  • Background workers opening excessive connections.
  • Missing connection pooling.
SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check active connections

SELECT
    state,
    COUNT(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY state;

Step 2: Identify applications consuming connections

SELECT
    application_name,
    client_addr,
    state,
    COUNT(*) AS connections
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY application_name, client_addr, state
ORDER BY connections DESC;

Step 3: Identify long-running connections

SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    application_name,
    state,
    now() - query_start AS duration,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY duration DESC;

Step 4: Terminate confirmed problematic sessions

SELECT pg_terminate_backend(12345);

Replace 12345 with the actual process ID after verifying that terminating the session is safe.

Recovery Strategy
  • Configure connection pooling using PgBouncer.
  • Set appropriate application pool limits.
  • Implement connection timeouts.
  • Close unused connections.
  • Investigate connection leaks.
  • Monitor active connections against max_connections.

Production Prevention: Establish connection budgets across all application instances rather than allowing every service to independently consume the entire database connection limit.

Related Reading: Explore PostgreSQL engineering resources on DevsCampus to learn more about PostgreSQL architecture, connection management, and production database operations.

2. PostgreSQL High CPU Utilization Incident Scenario

The PostgreSQL server suddenly reaches 95–100% CPU utilization.

Applications become slow, API requests time out, and database queries take significantly longer than usual.

Root Cause

High CPU utilization can result from:

  • Missing database indexes.
  • Expensive JOIN operations.
  • Inefficient SQL queries.
  • Large sequential scans.
  • Excessive concurrent queries.
  • Poor query execution plans.
  • Incorrect database statistics.
SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Identify expensive queries

SELECT
    pid,
    now() - query_start AS duration,
    state,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
ORDER BY duration DESC;

Step 2: Identify frequently executed expensive queries

If pg_stat_statements is enabled:

SELECT
    query,
    calls,
    total_exec_time,
    mean_exec_time,
    rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

Step 3: Analyze the execution plan

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1001;

Remember that EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query. Exercise caution with expensive queries and statements that modify data.

Step 4: Check server CPU usage

top

Or:

htop
Recovery Strategy
  • Identify and optimize expensive queries.
  • Add appropriate indexes.
  • Update database statistics using ANALYZE.
  • Reduce unnecessary query concurrency.
  • Review execution plans.
  • Consider read replicas for read-heavy workloads.

Production Prevention: Monitor query execution time, CPU utilization, and database workload continuously.

Related Reading: Learn how production database schemas influence query performance and scalability in Production Database Design on DevsCampus.

3. PostgreSQL Disk Space Exhaustion Incident Scenario

Your application starts reporting database write failures:

ERROR: could not extend file
No space left on device

Insert and update operations begin failing. PostgreSQL may also experience problems writing WAL files or temporary query files.

Root Cause

Common causes include:

  • Rapid database growth.
  • Unbounded application logs.
  • Large temporary files.
  • WAL accumulation.
  • Failed replication slots retaining WAL.
  • Missing WAL archiving cleanup.
  • Large database indexes.
  • Long-running transactions preventing cleanup.
SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check available disk space

df -h

Step 2: Identify large directories

sudo du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/*

Adjust the PostgreSQL data directory according to your installation.

Step 3: Check database sizes

SELECT
    datname,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(datname)) AS size
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY pg_database_size(datname) DESC;

Step 4: Check WAL directory size

sudo du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/*/pg_wal

Step 5: Check replication slots

SELECT
    slot_name,
    active,
    restart_lsn,
    pg_wal_lsn_diff(
        pg_current_wal_lsn(),
        restart_lsn
    ) AS retained_wal_bytes
FROM pg_replication_slots;
Recovery Strategy
  • Expand the underlying storage volume.
  • Investigate inactive replication slots.
  • Correct WAL archiving failures.
  • Review temporary file generation.
  • Remove only confirmed obsolete files through supported PostgreSQL maintenance procedures.
  • Implement database growth alerts.

Critical Warning: Never manually delete files from PostgreSQL's pg_wal directory. Doing so can cause database corruption or prevent PostgreSQL from starting.

Production Prevention: Configure disk usage alerts at 70%, 80%, and 90% capacity.

4. PostgreSQL Replication Lag Incident Scenario

Your production application uses PostgreSQL primary-replica architecture.

The primary database processes writes successfully, but read replicas return outdated data.

Users update their profiles but continue seeing old information.

Root Cause

Replication lag can occur because of:

  • Network latency.
  • High write throughput.
  • Slow replica storage.
  • Long-running queries on replicas.
  • Replication conflicts.
  • Insufficient replica resources.
  • WAL receiver or replay delays.
SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check replication status on the primary

SELECT
    application_name,
    client_addr,
    state,
    sync_state,
    write_lag,
    flush_lag,
    replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

Step 2: Check replication status on the replica

SELECT
    pg_is_in_recovery(),
    pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(),
    pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();

Step 3: Calculate replay delay

SELECT
    now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()
    AS replication_delay;

This timestamp-based calculation is most meaningful when the primary is actively committing transactions.

Recovery Strategy
  • Investigate network connectivity.
  • Increase replica compute and storage capacity where necessary.
  • Optimize queries running on replicas.
  • Investigate WAL receiver and replay activity.
  • Review replication configuration.
  • Temporarily route consistency-sensitive reads to the primary.

Production Prevention: Monitor replication lag and establish thresholds that trigger alerts before application consistency is affected.

5. PostgreSQL Deadlocks Incident Scenario

Your application starts reporting transaction failures:

ERROR: deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 1234 waits for ShareLock on transaction 5678

Multiple transactions are waiting for resources held by each other.

Root Cause

A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions wait indefinitely for locks held by one another.

Example:

Transaction A:

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 100
WHERE id = 2;

COMMIT;

Transaction B:

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 50
WHERE id = 2;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 50
WHERE id = 1;

COMMIT;

Both transactions acquire locks in different orders, potentially creating a deadlock.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Inspect database locks

SELECT
    locktype,
    relation::regclass,
    mode,
    granted,
    pid
FROM pg_locks
ORDER BY pid;

Step 2: Identify blocked queries

SELECT
    pid,
    pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocking_pids,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

Step 3: Inspect PostgreSQL logs

Look for:

ERROR: deadlock detected
Recovery Strategy
  • Acquire database locks in a consistent order.
  • Keep transactions short.
  • Avoid unnecessary operations inside transactions.
  • Implement application-level transaction retries.
  • Review transaction isolation requirements.

Production Prevention: Enable appropriate deadlock logging and monitor deadlock frequency.

6. PostgreSQL Slow Queries and Query Timeouts Incident Scenario

Your application starts experiencing intermittent API failures:

ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout

Some database queries take several seconds or even minutes to complete.

Root Cause

Common reasons include:

  • Missing indexes.
  • Inefficient joins.
  • Large table scans.
  • Outdated database statistics.
  • Lock contention.
  • Excessive sorting.
  • Poor pagination strategies.
SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Find long-running queries

SELECT
    pid,
    now() - query_start AS execution_time,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
ORDER BY execution_time DESC;

Step 2: Analyze query execution

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PENDING';

Step 3: Check table statistics

SELECT
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    n_dead_tup,
    last_analyze,
    last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables;

Step 4: Review timeout configuration

SHOW statement_timeout;
SHOW lock_timeout;
SHOW idle_in_transaction_session_timeout;
Recovery Strategy
  • Optimize problematic SQL.
  • Add appropriate indexes.
  • Review JOIN conditions.
  • Update statistics.
  • Investigate lock waits.
  • Apply sensible timeout limits.

Production Prevention: Use pg_stat_statements to identify queries with high total execution time and monitor query latency percentiles.

Related Reading: Learn more about production schema design, indexing considerations, and query scalability in Production Database Design – DevsCampus.

7. PostgreSQL Database Crash or Unexpected Restart Incident Scenario

Your production application suddenly loses database connectivity.

Monitoring reports:

Connection refused

The PostgreSQL service is no longer accepting connections.

Root Cause

Possible causes include:

  • Operating system out-of-memory termination.
  • Hardware failures.
  • Storage problems.
  • PostgreSQL process crashes.
  • Invalid configuration changes.
  • Container or Kubernetes restarts.
  • Host-level resource exhaustion.
SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check PostgreSQL service status

sudo systemctl status postgresql

Step 2: Inspect recent PostgreSQL logs

sudo journalctl -u postgresql \
    --since "30 minutes ago"

Depending on the distribution, PostgreSQL logs may also be available under:

/var/log/postgresql/

Step 3: Check memory utilization

free -h

Step 4: Check kernel OOM events

dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'oom|killed process'

Step 5: Check storage health

df -h
Recovery Strategy
  • Identify the actual crash reason before restarting repeatedly.
  • Verify storage availability.
  • Check memory and CPU pressure.
  • Review PostgreSQL recovery logs.
  • Restore service after confirming the underlying issue is resolved.
  • Validate application connectivity and transaction processing.

Production Prevention: Implement database health checks, infrastructure monitoring, automated backups, and tested recovery procedures.

8. PostgreSQL VACUUM Problems and Table Bloat Incident Scenario

Your database size keeps increasing even though application data is not growing significantly.

Queries become slower, indexes grow larger, and disk utilization increases.

Root Cause

PostgreSQL uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) to manage concurrent transactions.

Updates and deletes create obsolete row versions that must eventually be cleaned up by VACUUM.

Table bloat can increase when:

  • Autovacuum is disabled or incorrectly configured.
  • Long-running transactions prevent cleanup.
  • High update/delete workloads generate dead tuples.
  • Autovacuum cannot keep up with table modifications.
  • Replication slots or standby feedback retain old row versions.
SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Identify tables with dead tuples

SELECT
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    n_dead_tup,
    last_vacuum,
    last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC
LIMIT 10;

Step 2: Inspect autovacuum configuration

SHOW autovacuum;
SHOW autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor;
SHOW autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor;

Step 3: Identify long-running transactions

SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    state,
    now() - xact_start AS transaction_duration,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY transaction_duration DESC;
Recovery Strategy
  • Investigate long-running transactions.
  • Ensure autovacuum is enabled.
  • Tune autovacuum for large and frequently updated tables.
  • Run targeted VACUUM operations where appropriate. 
VACUUM (ANALYZE) orders;

For severe table bloat, evaluate specialized maintenance approaches such as pg_repack, accounting for locking, disk-space, and operational requirements.

Production Prevention: Monitor dead tuples, autovacuum activity, transaction age, and table growth.

Related Reading: PostgreSQL maintenance is essential for preventing table bloat and keeping query performance stable. Explore Database Maintenance on DevsCampus to understand VACUUM, ANALYZE, index maintenance, and database statistics in greater detail.

9. PostgreSQL WAL Growth and Checkpoint Problems Incident Scenario

Your database experiences increased disk utilization and write latency.

PostgreSQL logs contain messages related to checkpoints:

checkpoint starting: time
checkpoint complete

The WAL directory continues growing, and storage consumption becomes a concern.

Root Cause

Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) is essential for PostgreSQL durability and crash recovery.

WAL growth can result from:

  • High transaction volume.
  • Inactive replication slots.
  • WAL archiving failures.
  • Replication lag.
  • Long-running backups.
  • Incorrect WAL retention configuration.

Frequent checkpoints can also increase I/O pressure.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check WAL configuration

SHOW wal_level;
SHOW max_wal_size;
SHOW min_wal_size;
SHOW checkpoint_timeout;
SHOW checkpoint_completion_target;

Step 2: Check replication slot retention

SELECT
    slot_name,
    active,
    restart_lsn,
    wal_status
FROM pg_replication_slots;

Step 3: Check archiver statistics

SELECT
    archived_count,
    failed_count,
    last_archived_wal,
    last_failed_wal,
    last_failed_time
FROM pg_stat_archiver;

Step 4: Review PostgreSQL logs

Search for:

checkpoints are occurring too frequently
Recovery Strategy
  • Fix WAL archiving failures.
  • Investigate inactive replication slots.
  • Tune checkpoint settings based on workload.
  • Ensure storage capacity is sufficient.
  • Review replication and backup configurations.

Production Prevention: Monitor WAL generation rate, retained WAL, checkpoint frequency, and archiving failures.

Important: Never delete WAL files manually to free disk space.

10. PostgreSQL Backup and Recovery Failure Incident Scenario

A production database becomes corrupted or unavailable.

The SRE team attempts to restore the latest backup but discovers that the backup is incomplete, outdated, or unusable.

This is one of the most serious production incidents because it directly affects business continuity and data recovery.

Root Cause

Common reasons include:

  • Backup jobs silently failing.
  • Incorrect backup retention policies.
  • Missing WAL archives.
  • Unverified backup integrity.
  • Incomplete restore procedures.
  • Missing encryption keys.
  • Backups stored in the same failure domain as the database.
SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check backup availability

For pg_dump backups:

ls -lh /backup/postgres/

Step 2: Create a logical backup

pg_dump -Fc -U postgres \
    -d production_db \
    -f production_db.dump

Step 3: Validate the dump archive

pg_restore -l production_db.dump

This checks whether the archive can be listed, but it does not prove that a complete restore will succeed.

Step 4: Restore into a separate database

createdb -U postgres recovery_test

pg_restore -U postgres \
    -d recovery_test \
    production_db.dump

Step 5: Validate restored data

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM important_table;

Compare the results against expected records and application-level consistency checks.

Recovery Strategy
  • Maintain automated database backups.
  • Use continuous WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery (PITR).
  • Store backups in a separate failure domain.
  • Define Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO).
  • Perform regular restore drills.
  • Document disaster recovery procedures.

Production Prevention: A backup should never be considered reliable until a successful restore has been tested.

PostgreSQL SRE Incident Response: A Practical Framework

Knowing individual PostgreSQL failures is important, but production reliability requires a consistent incident response process.

SRE teams should follow a structured approach whenever a database outage occurs.

Step 1: Detect

Use monitoring and alerting tools to identify incidents before customers report them.

Monitor:

  • Database availability.
  • Active connections.
  • CPU utilization.
  • Memory utilization.
  • Disk utilization.
  • Query latency.
  • Replication lag.
  • WAL growth.
  • Deadlocks.
  • Database errors.
Step 2: Triage

Determine the impact and severity.

Ask:

  • Is the database completely unavailable?
  • Are writes failing or only reads?
  • Are all applications affected?
  • Is the problem isolated to one database or replica?
  • Is data integrity at risk?

Avoid making configuration changes before understanding the incident.

Step 3: Mitigate

Prioritize restoring critical application functionality.

Examples:

  • Terminate confirmed problematic sessions.
  • Route consistency-sensitive reads to the primary.
  • Scale infrastructure resources.
  • Reduce non-critical database workloads.
  • Restore available service capacity.

Always evaluate the impact of each mitigation action.

Step 4: Recover

After resolving the immediate issue:

  • Verify database health.
  • Validate application connectivity.
  • Test read and write operations.
  • Confirm replication health.
  • Check for data consistency issues.
  • Monitor the system for recurring failures.
Step 5: Conduct a Blameless Postmortem

Every major production incident should produce a postmortem.

A useful postmortem includes:

Section Description Incident Summary What happened? Timeline When did the incident begin and end? Impact Which services and customers were affected? Root Cause What technical condition caused the failure? Detection How was the incident identified? Resolution What actions restored service? Prevention What engineering improvements are required? Action Items Who owns each improvement and its deadline?

The goal is not to blame an engineer. The goal is to improve the system so the same failure is less likely to happen again.

Essential PostgreSQL Production Monitoring Metrics

A production-ready PostgreSQL environment should continuously monitor the following metrics.

Metric Why It Matters Active Connections Detect connection exhaustion CPU Utilization Identify expensive database workloads Memory Utilization Detect memory pressure Disk Utilization Prevent storage exhaustion Query Execution Time Identify slow SQL Replication Lag Detect replica synchronization problems Deadlocks Identify transaction conflicts Dead Tuples Detect vacuum-related issues WAL Generation Monitor write workload and WAL growth Checkpoint Frequency Identify excessive checkpoint activity Transaction Age Detect long-running transactions Backup Status Ensure recoverability
Recommended PostgreSQL Monitoring Tools 1. Prometheus and Grafana

Use Prometheus with PostgreSQL Exporter to collect database metrics and Grafana to build operational dashboards.

2. pg_stat_statements

A PostgreSQL extension that provides statistics about SQL query execution.

3. PgBouncer

A lightweight connection pooler that helps manage database connection overhead.

4. pgBadger

A PostgreSQL log analyzer that helps identify slow queries and database workload patterns.

5. Patroni

A high-availability solution for managing PostgreSQL clusters with automated failover capabilities.

Learn More: Production Database Monitoring

Monitoring is one of the most important responsibilities of an SRE team. Identifying performance degradation before it becomes a production outage requires more than checking whether a database is online.

Explore Production Database Monitoring on DevsCampus to understand:

  • Database latency and p99 query performance.
  • Active and available database connections.
  • Replication lag monitoring.
  • Cache and buffer hit ratios.
  • Lock waits and deadlock detection.
  • Table and index bloat monitoring.
  • Production database alerting strategies.

This learning resource complements the troubleshooting runbooks covered in this article.

PostgreSQL Production Readiness Checklist

Before deploying PostgreSQL into production, validate the following:

Availability
  • [ ] Configure appropriate connection pooling.
  • [ ] Implement database health checks.
  • [ ] Configure replication where required.
  • [ ] Define failover procedures.
Performance
  • [ ] Enable pg_stat_statements.
  • [ ] Monitor slow queries.
  • [ ] Review index usage.
  • [ ] Configure autovacuum appropriately.
Storage
  • [ ] Configure disk utilization alerts.
  • [ ] Monitor WAL growth.
  • [ ] Monitor replication slots.
  • [ ] Review backup retention policies.
Security
  • [ ] Use strong authentication.
  • [ ] Apply least-privilege database permissions.
  • [ ] Enable encrypted connections.
  • [ ] Store database credentials securely.
  • [ ] Audit privileged database access.
Disaster Recovery
  • [ ] Automate backups.
  • [ ] Configure point-in-time recovery where required.
  • [ ] Define RPO and RTO.
  • [ ] Perform regular restore tests.
  • [ ] Document disaster recovery runbooks.
Conclusion

PostgreSQL production outages are not always caused by database crashes. Many incidents originate from connection exhaustion, inefficient queries, storage pressure, replication lag, transaction conflicts, or inadequate backup strategies.

For SREs and database engineers, the ability to identify symptoms, investigate root causes, and execute safe recovery procedures is critical.

The ten incident scenarios covered in this guide provide a practical starting point for building reliable PostgreSQL operations.

However, production reliability is not achieved by troubleshooting incidents alone. It requires continuous monitoring, capacity planning, automation, tested disaster recovery procedures, and a culture of learning from failures.

Remember: A production-ready database is not simply one that runs without errors. It is one that can detect failures, recover safely, and maintain data integrity when things go wrong.
